before.name: Southeast Slopes
before.fa: Bill Cox and Will F. Thompson (1938)
gear: microspikes or crampons — snow lingers in the Access Col/Luna Pass gullies well into July
optional 30–35m rope and a few slings/light pro for parties wanting a running belay across the false-to-true-summit traverse (most parties solo this unroped in normal summer conditions)
bear canister (free loaner available at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount)
insect head net — mosquitoes and ground-nesting bees are common in the forested approach
hazards: extreme remoteness — a multi-day, largely off-trail approach with no cell coverage; a serious injury near the summit realistically requires helicopter evacuation, not a ground carry-out
brushy, steep approach through the Access Creek basin choked with devil's club and slide alder; the first off-trail quarter-mile alone can take over an hour
cold, thigh-to-waist-deep fords of Big Beaver Creek and Access Creek
lingering snow/ice in the gullies to Access Col and on Luna Pass well into July
~4,000 ft of sustained, continuous exposure on the Class 3–4 traverse between the false and true summits
sparse cairns and genuine route-finding difficulty across the cross-country basins in poor visibility
ground-nesting bees/wasps encountered by multiple parties in the forested sections
before.overview: Luna Peak is the highest summit of the Picket Range and a coveted viewpoint over the savage skyline of the Southern and Northern Pickets. First climbed in September 1938 by Bill Cox and Will F. Thompson, it is also one of Washington's highest-prominence peaks (required for the WA 2,000+ ft prominence list). No maintained trail reaches the mountain — the standard line is a long, remote, largely off-trail approach via Big Beaver and Access Creek, making this one of the more committing 'moderate' summits in the Cascades despite its modest Class 3 technical grade.
before.beta: Access from Luna Cirque via Access Creek, ascend steep gullies to southeast ridge, traverse to southwest ridge with exposed Class 3 summit traverse on loose rock. Crux is 5 feet exposed between false and true summit.
before.turnaround: Plan to summit by early afternoon for safe descent. Do not continue if more than 2 hours from summit by 2 PM. Weather deteriorates rapidly; 15-minute window can close within minutes.
before.rock_grade: Class 2-3 (Class 3 on the exposed summit traverse)
before.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
before.comms: Cell/satellite communication absent in remote Picket Range. Satellite messengers (InReach, spot) strongly recommended for emergency use. Contact rangers before departure.
before.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb the Class 3–4 traverse to the false summit, descend the broad ridge's Class 2 talus (~1,100 ft) back to Luna Pass, then retrace the basin traverse, Access Col gully, and Access Creek/Big Beaver Creek fords back to the Big Beaver Trail.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: SR 20 MP 134 pullout (4 cars + 2 ADA spots), just past the winter closure gate; no day-use fee, but a backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center is required to camp.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead pullout at milepost 134, around 2,050 feet, just past the winter closure gate — room for about four cars plus two ADA spots, and no day-use fee. From the trailhead, an 0.8-mile trail drops to Ross Lake, where a boat shuttle covers roughly nine miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead: the seasonal Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a paddled canoe or packraft if you don't have a shuttle reservation. The shuttle's season and hours govern when you can actually reach the trailhead, so check its schedule before planning dates — it typically runs late May through early October. Camping requires a backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam / Ross Lake crossing
waypoints.note: Trail drops 0.8 mi to Ross Dam; cross the dam and either hike the Ross Lake shoreline or catch the seasonal water taxi (reserve through Ross Lake Resort) north to the Big Beaver Trailhead.

waypoints.name: 39 Mile Camp
waypoints.note: Small 3-site camp on Big Beaver Creek near a stand of ancient red cedars; water at the 39 Mile Creek crossing, no bear box so hang food carefully.

waypoints.name: Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Last maintained-trail camp before leaving Big Beaver Trail; onward travel to Access Creek is off-trail bushwhacking.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Creek ford / Access Creek brush
waypoints.note: Waist-deep ford of Big Beaver Creek (a logjam crossing exists downstream) followed by dense alder-swath bushwhacking up the Access Creek drainage.

waypoints.name: Access Creek Basin
waypoints.note: Boulder-strewn basin used as base camp, with a flat-top boulder as a common tent platform; last reliable water before the high traverse to Luna Pass.

waypoints.name: Luna Pass
waypoints.note: Gains the Luna Cirque high country via the Access Couloir/Col; established tent sites 50 ft above the pass to the north mark the start of the southeast-slopes scramble.

waypoints.name: Luna Peak
waypoints.note: From the Class 2-3 false summit, downclimb the exposed Class 4 chimney then traverse narrow ledges on the east face (running belay recommended) to the true summit.

before.detailed_rack: Optional: 50-60m rope for belayed crux; many solo. Minimal rock gear.
pro_tips: Reserve the seasonal Ross Lake Resort water taxi to the Big Beaver trailhead — it cuts up to ~14 round-trip miles of lakeshore walking versus hiking from Ross Dam
Camp on the flat boulder/heather bench in the upper Access Creek basin (~3,900–4,500 ft) to shorten summit day and get the brush behind you early
Borrow a free bear canister at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount when picking up your permit
Book your Recreation.gov backcountry permit as soon as the season opens (late April) — the Access Creek/Luna Camp zone quotas fill fast for summer weekends
watch_out: The false-summit-to-true-summit traverse looks intimidating from a distance but is only Class 3–4 on solid rock — most parties do it unroped; needing a rope here is generally a sign to turn around, not to push on
Devil's club and slide alder in the Access Creek brush hide slick logs and holes — expect slow going and consider gaiters/long sleeves
Big Beaver and Access Creek fords are cold and can run thigh-to-waist deep even in August after a warm spell
Cairns are sparse across the cross-country basins between Access Col and Luna Pass; a whiteout here makes route-finding genuinely difficult
Mosquitoes are thick at the Luna Lake camps and in the upper basins in early July; bring a head net.
before.pro_needs: Varies by experience. Single 50m rope with harness/slings for crux. Self-rescue knowledge essential.
before.best_season: Late July through September gives the most reliable snow-free travel on the approach gullies and summit traverse. Strong parties with scrambling/glacier travel experience have climbed as early as late June, carrying an ice axe and microspikes/crampons for lingering snow on Access Col and Luna Pass. The Ross Lake Resort water taxi, which meaningfully shortens the approach, operates only roughly June through October.
before.approach: The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR 20 (North Cascades Highway, ~2,050ft), where parking is right off the highway. From there it's about a 0.8-mile hike down the Ross Dam Trail to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a paddled canoe/packraft for parties without a shuttle reservation) roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead (~1,600ft) near the Big Beaver / 39 Mile camp area — this lake crossing is a key logistical step, not an afterthought, since Ross Lake Resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can actually reach the trailhead. From the Big Beaver Trailhead, follow the Big Beaver Trail through old-growth cedar forest along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek for about 8 miles to Luna Camp (an established backcountry campsite, permit required from the NPS backcountry office), gaining only modest elevation on generally mellow, well-graded tread. Continue north on the Big Beaver Trail roughly 1.5 more miles past Luna Camp; watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek (~2,460ft) — this is the turn onto the Access Creek approach. Ford Big Beaver Creek here (can run high with snowmelt in early season) and pick up the boot path along the north flank of Access Creek through semi-open forest. Around 3,700ft the brush thickens substantially; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint climbers' path use talus benches to avoid the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This creek-drainage stretch is the approach crux: expect sustained bushwhacking, blowdown, and route-finding, and budget real time for it. The path deposits you in the open upper basin at the Access Creek headwaters (~4,400ft), a common base-camp location roughly 1,700ft above Luna Camp. From camp, ascend broad talus (snow-filled early season) gullies southwest toward an obvious gap in the ridge above; once on the ridge, traverse south of Point 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's SE side, then cross that basin at about the 6,600ft level to Luna Col (7,200ft), the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. There is no reliable water above Access Creek camp except lingering snowmelt, so tank up before the final push.
before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly — there is no rappelling on this route and no shorter alternative down-route; it is a walk-off/downclimb from summit to camp. From the true (east) summit, reverse the short, exposed Class 3 traverse and the 5-foot downclimb step across the notch back to the false (south) summit, then descend the broad Class 2 talus ridge about 1,100 feet to Luna Col. From the col, reverse the basin traverse at ~6,600ft, cross back over the ridge south of Point 6,730, and downclimb the talus/snow gully into the Access Creek headwaters basin to regain camp. The next day (or continuing the same push on a car-to-car attempt), retrace the Access Creek boot path — staying on the south bank through the brushy 3,700ft band before recrossing to the north flank lower down — back to the Big Beaver Trail, ford Big Beaver Creek, and hike the 8 miles out to the Big Beaver Trailhead, then take the boat shuttle/paddle back down Ross Lake and hike up to the Ross Dam Trailhead. Watch for loose talus and scree underfoot on the upper ridge descent (rockfall risk onto parties below), and treat the Access Creek brush band as slower and more disorienting on tired legs going down than it was on the way up — several parties note losing the boot path here in poor light. No technical rope work, fixed anchors, or rappel stations exist anywhere on this route; a rope is occasionally carried for the exposed summit step in early-season/icy conditions but is used, if at all, as a handline rather than for rappelling.
before.bail: Retreat means reversing the lengthy approach; commit only with stable weather and adequate supplies.

pitch_detail.notes: High camp near Access Creek headwaters (~3,650-4,100 ft) up scree/talus and a dirt-filled gully to a col near 5,800-6,300 ft.
Heather, talus, and snowfield traverse across southeast-facing slopes to Luna Pass (~7,200 ft).
Continue across the southeast slopes from Luna Pass to the false summit, staying off the broad south ridge.

~500 ft of loose, exposed ridge from the false summit to the true summit; one party reported a ~15 ft Class 4 chimney off the false summit followed by narrow ledges. Following east-side ledges avoids most Class 4 moves.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP requires a backcountry wilderness permit for the Access Creek camp; Ross Lake Resort's water taxi, which saves ~6 miles of lakeshore hiking, typically runs late May through early October.

days.note: A long approach day: drop to Ross Lake and take the water taxi (or walk the lakeshore trail) to the Big Beaver trailhead, then follow the Big Beaver Trail roughly 10-11 miles past Luna Camp before leaving maintained trail to bushwhack and boulder-hop up the brushy Access Creek drainage to a high camp near 4,300-4,500 ft.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee for advance backcountry reservations (walk-up permits carry no fee). No park entrance fee. The Ross Lake Resort water taxi is a separate optional paid service (~$35 round trip per person, seasonal).
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: A bear canister or approved food storage is required where a proper hang isn't possible; free loaner canisters are available at the Wilderness Information Center. Practice Leave No Trace; off-trail cross-country travel is legal in this zone but stay on rock/snow/durable surfaces where possible to protect fragile heather meadows.
access.permit: A backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay, year-round. Reserve in advance on Recreation.gov (the general on-sale window opens around 7 a.m. Pacific in late April) or apply for a walk-up permit; permits must be picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. The Access Creek/Luna Camp zones carry limited nightly quotas and fill for summer weekends.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam Trailhead gate (MP 134) and the Silver Star/Early Winters gate (roughly MP 171–178), typically early December through mid-April, cutting off road access to the trailhead itself. The Ross Lake Resort water taxi runs seasonally, roughly June through October. Luna Fire closure (as of mid-September 2026): the Big Beaver Trail is closed from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, and Luna Camp, Beaver Pass Camp (with its stock and group camps) and 39 Mile Camp (with 39 Mile Stock) are closed; cross-country zone access from closed trails is prohibited. The closure moves - check current park fire closures before a trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone), fee per person, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Hannegan-side permits can also be picked up at the Glacier Public Service Center on its limited summer days.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR 20) to Ross Dam Trailhead, MP 134
road.driveNote: Trailhead parking sits right at the highway; from the trailhead, descend about 0.8 mile to Ross Dam to reach the lakeshore trail or the Ross Lake Resort water taxi dock.
road.seasonalGate: Closes for winter roughly early December through mid-April between the Ross Dam Trailhead gate (MP 134) and the Silver Star/Early Winters gate (MP ~171–178); exact opening date varies year to year with snowpack and road repairs

climate.typical: Remote maritime alpine climate with a narrow midsummer-to-early-fall window.

bySeason.fall: Shorter days, colder; early storms possible
bySeason.spring: Heavy snow, avalanche terrain, impractical access
bySeason.summer: Main season once brush and snow consolidate; long daylight helps

emergency.notes: The summit is 15+ trail/off-trail miles from the nearest road; a serious injury near the summit realistically requires an NPS/county helicopter evacuation. Cell coverage is essentially nonexistent throughout the approach — carry a satellite messenger and file a wilderness trip plan.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA 98267 — (360) 854-7245
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Dr, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284 — roughly 46 road miles / about 1 hour drive from the Ross Dam Trailhead via SR 20

crowds.peakTraffic: If any at all, would be clustered in August during peak Picket Range traverse/climbing season
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - likely only a handful to a few dozen parties per season; among the least-traveled named peaks in the Cascades

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - roundtrip is roughly 48 miles including on-trail travel, ~5 miles of bushwhacking, and miles of scree/talus/heather, typically spread over 3-4 days
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy multi-day overnight pack (food, camp, and travel gear) carried over brush, talus, and creek crossings

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day approach (commonly 2+ days each way) via Ross Lake/Big Beaver and the Access Creek drainage into Luna Cirque before the summit push
requiredSkills: basic snow travel for lingering snowfields on the approach and SE shoulder
wilderness backcountry camping and Leave No Trace practice
self-sufficient route-finding with no reliable trail for much of the approach
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Seasoned backcountry mountaineer/scrambler with prior multi-day wilderness expedition experience; not a route for a first alpine partner

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, once brush has leafed out and lingering snow has consolidated

July.reason: Early in the window - approach brush may still be wet/thick and snow can linger in the SE-facing chutes and on the shoulder, so snow travel skill is more likely needed

August.reason: Most consolidated conditions of the year - brush cleared, snowfields mostly melted out, long daylight for the long approach

September.reason: Often stable weather before fall storms arrive, but shorter days and colder temps reduce margin on the long approach and exposed traverse

weather.typical: Remote maritime alpine climate with a narrow midsummer-to-early-fall climbing window; summers are the main viable season while spring carries heavy snow and impractical access
weather.probability: Early fall storms can arrive by mid-September and cut the season short; multi-day forecasts are essential given the multi-day approach

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Loose Class 2-3 talus/scree exposes parties below to rockfall; the short Class 4 traverse between the false (south) summit and true summit is exposed with real fall consequences and is the technical crux of an otherwise non-technical route

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route in the North Cascades NP interior; no NWAC forecast zone provides point coverage for this remote location

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on the standard Southeast Slopes route

gaps: No confirmed guidebook (Beckey Cascade Alpine Guide) page citation located for this exact route line

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Newhalem, drive SR-20 east about 14 miles; the trailhead parking is on the right between mileposts 134 and 135.

before.rope_type: 30m optional (glacier/snow travel, not typically used on rock)
before.rope_note: Standard SE approach ascends scree/rubble climber's right to a steep snow-filled chute onto Luna's SE shoulder and Luna Col (7,200 ft); ice axe and microspikes/aluminum crampons needed year-round for the snow chute. The route itself is usually unroped, but some parties carry a short rope for the glaciated approach snowfields and the Class 3-4 summit block shared with the South Ridge route.

approach_variants.name: Access Creek basin, then the gap south of Point 6,730 and the 6,600 ft basin traverse to Luna Col
approach_variants.notes:
The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at about 2,050 ft, with parking right off the highway. About 0.8 mile of trail leads down to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft. The lake crossing is a logistical step rather than an afterthought, since the resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can reach the trailhead at all.

From the Big Beaver Trailhead, about 8 miles of well-graded trail through old-growth cedar along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek reach Luna Camp. Continue roughly 1.5 miles past it and watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek at about 2,460 ft. Ford Big Beaver Creek there.

Around 3,700 ft the brush thickens; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint path use talus benches to dodge the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This stretch is the approach crux. The path deposits you in the open basin at the Access Creek headwaters at about 4,400 ft, the common base camp.
hazards: Sustained bushwhacking, blowdown and route-finding in the Access Creek drainage, the approach crux
A ford of Big Beaver Creek that can run high with snowmelt
A narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest between the false and true summits, with cliffs on both sides
Loose talus and scree on the upper ridge with rockfall risk onto parties below
No reliable water above the Access Creek camp except lingering snowmelt
Losing the boot path in poor light on the way down, which several trip reports record
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route contours where the south ridge climbs, and the difference starts above camp rather than at the col. From the Access Creek basin, ascend broad talus gullies, snow-filled early season, southwest toward an obvious gap in the ridge above. Once on the ridge, traverse south of point 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's southeast side, then cross that basin at about the 6,600 ft level to Luna Col at 7,200 ft.

So the fog test is an altimeter test: the basin crossing is held at roughly 6,600 ft. Losing height into the basin or gaining it toward the crest both cost you, and both are what happens when you navigate by feel. Hold the contour and it delivers you to the col.

Arrival: Luna Col at 7,200 ft is the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. You are there when the ground drops away on the far side.

Confirm on the climb, and the count is short: above the col the route is roughly 1,100 ft of class 2-3 talus and scree to the false, southern summit, then one short connecting ridge to the true summit. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left at the false summit.

The one technical spot, and its tell: drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit onto a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest with a snow-covered cliff falling several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff dropping the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the worst of it by dropping onto a ledge on the southeast side and scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit. If you are on a crest with snow on your left and bare rock on your right, you are in the right place and there is one short section of it.

No water above the access creek basin. The summit push is done on what you carry.

climbing_route.label: Broad ridge to the false summit
climbing_route.notes: From Luna Col at about 7,200 ft the route climbs the broad ridge above on roughly 1,100 ft of class 2 to 3 talus and scree to the false, southern summit. The rock is loose in places and parties are advised not to stack up beneath one another. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left here.

climbing_route.label: Connecting ridge to the true summit
climbing_route.notes: The true summit lies beyond a short connecting ridge that is the only technical part of the peak. Drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit and scramble a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest: a snow-covered cliff falls several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff drops the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the most exposed traverse by dropping onto a ledge on the southeast side, scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit and finishing with a few 4th-class moves from the back. Descent reverses the route; there is no water above the Access Creek basin, so the summit push is done on what you carry.

bivy.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
bivy.notes: The open basin at the top of the Access Creek approach, roughly 1,700 ft above Luna Camp and the standard base for the peak. Getting here is the hard part: valley-bottom devil's club, a crossing to the north bank, then a swap back to the south side near 3,700-3,800 ft where cairns and a faint path use talus benches to duck the worst slide alder. Reports put the bushwhack alone at around three hours on the way out. From camp the climb goes up talus gullies southwest to a gap in the ridge, south of Point 6,730 on heather benches, then across the basin at about 6,600 ft to Luna Col at 7,200 ft — some 4,000 ft of gain, all of it above the last dependable water, so tank up before leaving.
bivy.water: Access Creek at the head of the drainage; reliable, but it is the last water until lingering snowmelt higher up
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. Cross-country camping is only allowed on durable surfaces — snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadows, and never within 100 ft of water
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground; parties describe it as pleasant camping for a small group rather than a set of established sites

bivy.name: Luna Camp (Big Beaver Trail)
bivy.notes: The signed camp about 8 miles up the Big Beaver Trail from the boat landing, in old-growth cedar and only modestly above lake level. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it earns its place because the water-taxi timetable often puts you on the trail late. From here it is another 1.5 miles north to the easy-to-miss boot path that leaves the trail just above the Access Creek confluence, so sleeping here sets you up to start the bushwhack fresh rather than at dusk.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek, right there and reliable
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for every overnight in the park complex, picked up from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount; Luna Camp is a designated site, not cross-country ground
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp with a fixed number of sites; your permit itinerary names the camp and the night

keptBefore.name: Southwest Ridge
keptBefore.approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134), cross Ross Dam and work around the lake to the Big Beaver Trail, or save about 7 miles by taking the lake boat shuttle to Big Beaver landing. Follow Big Beaver Trail past Luna Camp, roughly 10 miles up from the landing, and leave it about 1.5 miles beyond the camp at a big cairn on the left. Drop through forest to Big Beaver Creek, ford it since logs are not dependable, then traverse southwest through alder thickets to the head of Access Creek, crossing it near 3900 ft and camping in the meadow near 4200 ft. From there climb about 2000 ft of loose gully to the col that opens onto the southwest ridge, and make an ascending traverse to the next col at the edge of the ridge, where the climbing starts.
keptBefore.descent_text: Descend the way you came. From the summit, work back along the ramps and ledges on the southeast side to the false summit, then downclimb the class 3 rock of the southwest ridge to the col. The step between the two summits is very exposed and a fall there would be fatal, so move carefully and avoid wet rock. From the col, retrace the traverse to the upper col and descend the gully to the Access Creek meadows, which becomes a loose rock pile late in the season, so stay close together or out of each other's fall line and wear helmets. Then bushwhack back to Big Beaver Creek, ford it, and walk the Big Beaver trail out to the Ross Lake landing.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Newhalem, drive SR-20 east about 14 miles; the trailhead parking is on the right between mileposts 134 and 135.

before.name: West Face
before.fa: Ray Clough and Charles Kirschner, July 10, 1938

set.best_season: Ski ascents run late March through May, best in April and early May when the snow is stable and softens to corn. On foot, July through mid-August is the usual window, while the glaciers are still snow-covered and bridged. From mid-August into September crevasses open wide and Winnie's Slide turns to bare ice.

before.name: White Salmon Glacier
before.fa: Piley, Richards, Thompson — September 9, 1926 (spelling of names unverified)
before.description: Easy snow approach via White Salmon Glacier. Straightforward glacier climb with minimal technical difficulty. Gains roughly 7,500 ft car to car.
gear: Rope for glacier travel and for belaying/short-pitching the steeper sections
Crevasse rescue kit — the route winds around crevasses and outcroppings on the White Salmon Glacier itself
Pickets — Winnies Slide (40-45°, ~6,800 ft) is steep enough that many parties want protection there rather than soloing it
Awareness of late-season bergschrund difficulty crossing onto Curtis Glacier; an ice screw or two is worth carrying for that transition if the schrund is open
hazards: Avalanches off the Hanging Glacier onto the approach/glacier.
Crevasses on Curtis and White Salmon Glaciers, worse late season.
before.overview: An easy glacier ascent/descent on Shuksan's north side, often used as the descent for northside routes and a moderate ski/snow climb in its own right.
before.beta: Grade II glacier route (easy snow), up to 40-45 degree snow. Route to summit via Winnies Slide (40-45 degree snow) or Fisher Chimneys junction. 3rd-4th class scrambling on the summit pyramid. Active Hanging Glacier avalanches. Bergschrunds, crevasses.
before.turnaround: Turn around before afternoon warming increases avalanche hazard from the active Hanging Glacier above the approach valley.
before.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
before.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the glacier or approach valley.
before.descent: Reverse the route; it is the most common descent for northside Shuksan climbs (North Face, Northeast Ridge, Hanging Glacier).
obj_haz: large avalanches off the very active Hanging Glacier into the approach valley
party-induced rockfall in the central gully

waypoints.name: White Salmon Lodge road gate (Mount Baker Highway hairpin)
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 18 miles to the hairpin switchback at roughly 3,500 ft, below the ski area, and park in the small pull-off at the gated White Salmon Road (FS 3075). Parking is very limited and is not allowed on the highway shoulder; do not block the gate. No parking pass is required.

waypoints.name: White Salmon Glacier toe
waypoints.note: Glacier travel begins where the road/approach ends.
waypoints.directions: Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the White Salmon Lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the glacier's toe; without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom.

waypoints.name: White Salmon Glacier
waypoints.directions: Rope up and climb the White Salmon Glacier, weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses. The basin below sits under the active Hanging Glacier, whose avalanches can sweep it, so move through early and don't linger.

waypoints.name: Winnie's Slide
waypoints.note: 150-200 ft step of steep 40-45° snow/ice onto the Upper Curtis Glacier; schrund can be tricky late season.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the glacier among the outcrops to the foot of Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft, the only abrupt steepening on this side of the mountain.

waypoints.name: Hell's Highway
waypoints.note: Snow chute connecting to the west edge of the Sulphide Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb Winnie's Slide, about 150-200 ft of 40-45 degree snow that can be hard snow or ice late season, onto the Upper Curtis Glacier. Cross the Upper Curtis southward: it starts steep, eases, then loses height to the base of Hell's Highway. Keep the rope tight as crevasses open through the summer.

waypoints.name: Mount Shuksan
waypoints.directions: Climb Hell's Highway, a short chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, watching for a moat where snow meets rock, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid and finish by the central gully on its south face (3rd-4th class) or the West Ridge (4th class).

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning to cross glaciers on firm snow

before.detailed_rack: No rock rack needed for the standard line; carry crevasse-rescue and glacier travel gear.
what_to_bring: extra layers for the exposed traverse near Hell's Highway
pro_tips: This is probably the most common descent route for northside Shuksan climbs, so know it even if climbing something else.
In April the narrowest part of the final summit gully was easier on the climber's left than on the right.
watch_out: Glacier climbing with crevasse hazard present
Early turnaround essential - sun softening increases hazard
In early April a big avalanche debris field can choke the White Salmon creek drainage; budget about an hour to wind through it
before.pro_needs: Glacier travel protection (pickets, screws in late-season ice) rather than rock gear.
before.best_season: Ski ascents run late March through May, best in April and early May when the snow is stable and softens to corn. On foot, July through mid-August is the usual window, while the glaciers are still snow-covered and bridged. From mid-August into September crevasses open wide and Winnie's Slide turns to bare ice.
before.approach: From the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom. Bivy sites sit among the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the glacier.
before.descent_text: Downclimb the glacier back through Hell's Highway, across Curtis Glacier, down Winnie's Slide, and out around the clearcut to the White Salmon pull-off.
before.bail: Retreat down the glacier the way you came; no fixed bail points.

pitch_detail.notes: From the bivy among the rock outcrops on the glacier's east edge, rope up and climb the White Salmon Glacier, weaving around outcrops and crevasses to the foot of Winnie's Slide near 6,800 ft. The valley below and this lower glacier sit under the very active Hanging Glacier, whose avalanches can sweep the whole area, so move through early and don't linger.

Climb Winnie's Slide, a short, steep snow slope of about 40-45 degrees, roughly one rope length (150-200 ft), until you can step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier. Late season it can be hard snow or ice, when an ice screw or two for protection makes sense. It is often downclimbed in a boot pack on the way out.

Cross the Upper Curtis Glacier southward: it starts steep, eases, then loses height to the base of Hell's Highway. Early on the crevasses are well bridged; by late summer they open wide and the bridges weaken, so keep the rope tight.

Climb Hell's Highway, a short (about 60 m) chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Watch for a moat where snow meets rock. Then follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid.

Finish on the summit pyramid by the central gully on its south face (3rd-4th class, steep snow early season) or by the West Ridge (4th class). The gully sheds loose rock under traffic late in the season. Descend the gully, then reverse Hell's Highway, the Curtis Glacier and Winnie's Slide.

access.fees: No climbing fee (Forest Service approach). An NPS permit is required if camping overnight past the park boundary, and it is not free: $10 per person plus a $6 fee, youth 15 and under free.
access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required ($5/day or $30/annual). No specific climbing permit.
access.rules: Same MBS NF rules as Mount Baker (fire/camping setbacks near named trails/lakes, pack out human waste). Parties are limited to 12 people in the park's cross-country zones around Shuksan.
access.seasonal: The Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) is plowed year-round to the Mt. Baker Ski Area, near where this approach starts; the road beyond to Artist Point is closed in winter.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for any camp inside the park - quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit at the Glacier Public Service Center (in season) or the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Camps below the park boundary, such as Lake Ann and lower Shannon Ridge, are in the Mount Baker Wilderness and need only the free self-issue permit at the trailhead.

road.name: Mount Baker Highway (SR-542)
road.status: Paved; plowed year-round to the Mt. Baker Ski Area
road.driveNote: White Salmon pull-off is at a hairpin switchback ~18 miles east of Glacier, just past milepost 51, near White Salmon Road (FS-3075).
road.seasonalGate: Closed by winter snow beyond the ski area

climate.summer: Crevasses open up as the season progresses
climate.winter: Not a climbing season; avalanche terrain
climate.typical: Marine alpine climate, heavy winter snowpack

emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades NP Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, (360) 854-7245
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth St. Joseph Medical Center, Bellingham, WA
emergency.sheriffDispatch: North Cascades NP SAR (360) 856-5700 ext. 515; after-hours (360) 873-4590 ext. 37; Whatcom County Sheriff (360) 676-6911

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June to mid-July, while snow still bridges the creek valley and the glacier's crevasses before they open up

May.reason: Firm snow runs from the road-end clearcut to the glacier, but spring avalanche cycles off the Hanging Glacier and basin slopes are still active.

July.reason: Snow recedes from the valley bottom and the clearcut contour gets brushier, but crevasses on the White Salmon are usually still bridged early in the month.

June.reason: Deep snow still fills the creek valley and bridges most crevasses, so the approach avoids slide alder; cross under the Hanging Glacier early.

April.reason: In early April with a deep base the glaciers can be travelled unroped; crampons came out for the Upper Curtis Glacier and the upper part of Hell's Highway, and the snow in the summit gully was firm at midday.

August.reason: The approach becomes a brushy contour with stream crossings, and crevasses on the White Salmon and Curtis glaciers open, lengthening route-finding.

October.reason: Shortening days, first autumn snow over open crevasses, and wet brush on the approach make this a poor time for the glacier.

September.reason: Bare, broken glacier and open crevasses make travel slow and circuitous, and the summit pyramid scramble is looser once snow is gone.

approach_logistics.trailhead: White Salmon Lodge road gate (Mount Baker Highway hairpin)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: At the hairpin on the Mount Baker Highway near mile 52, below the ski area, park in the small pull-off at the gated road to White Salmon Lodge. Don't block the gate.

before.rope_type: single 30m glacier rope (or 60m if combining with Winnies Slide/Fisher Chimneys exit)
before.rope_note: Complex glacier route with short 1-2 pitch snow/rock/ice sections crossing bergschrunds; joins Winnies Slide about 2/3 height. Requires solid belaying and moderate ice technique.
before.corrections: Grade II/easy-snow characterization from the route list is a bit generous — sources describe short technical ice/rock steps requiring real belaying skill, not a walk-up.
rack: Single 30m glacier rope (or 60m combined with Fisher Chimneys exit)

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road
approach_variants.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.
hazards: avalanche off the Hanging Glacier across the approach basin
brush in the valley bottom without snow cover
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
Winnie's Slide holds firm ice when it has melted back
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route proper begins at the foot of the White Salmon Glacier, or from the bivy sites up and right of it. Ascend the glacier weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses; the marker you are climbing toward is the base of Winnie's Slide at roughly 6,800 ft. Winnie's Slide is unmistakable once you are under it — the angle jumps to around forty to forty-five degrees for roughly a rope length, and it is the only thing on this side of the mountain that steepens like that. Above it you step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier.

If you are still on low-angle glacier threading around rock islands, you are below the slide, however long you have been walking. Conversely, if you have topped out on flatter glacier without a steep pitch behind you, you have drifted off the line and are somewhere else on the White Salmon.

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.
hazards: a committing descent at the start that must be reclimbed on the way out
Hanging Glacier avalanche debris across the valley
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Winter or spring on skis, when a party planning a ski descent starts from the ski area base and traverses down into the creek valley rather than walking the old road.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft is still the reference feature low on the route; higher, the head of the White Salmon is marked by the base of Hell's Highway. Neither is a subtle feature — both are abrupt steepenings out of low-angle glacier.

bivy.name: Rock outcrop bivy, east edge of the lower White Salmon Glacier
bivy.notes: Bivy on the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the White Salmon Glacier near its foot. Camp here rather than in the approach valley, which is under icefall from the Hanging Glacier.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit
bivy.capacity: Small flat spots among rock outcrops; a few tents

bivy.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
bivy.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide
